It was the checks.

We gave away $5,000 and $10,000 to three of our SaaS Suite customers: Andy Griffith, Susie Guzman and Muneo Dongo. Real people who took the platform, built a real business on it, and showed up.

Therefore that's what I'm taking home from this week: the stage is nice, but the customer stories are the whole point. Every feature we ship is only worth what someone builds with it.

Thank you to everyone who stopped by the booth, signed the board, and grabbed a photo. And thank you to the HighLevel team for having us.

items.title: LinkedIn: Picture a gym owner who wants an online store.
items.body:
_Note: scenario is illustrative (demo funnel = a gym), not a real client story — swap in a real one if Andrew has it._
_Angle: what changed. Image: carousel slide 1 or the before/after funnel-steps screenshot._

Picture a gym owner who wants an online store.

Not a big one. Day passes, a few shirts, a protein tub.

Until now the answer was usually "Shopify," but that means another login, another bill, and another tool their HighLevel setup can't see.

So open their funnel instead.

One element. A cart icon, dropped into the header. HighLevel asks which sections you want to carry over — hero, gallery, testimonials, FAQ, footer — and you click Import.

Therefore their one-page funnel becomes a store: product list, product details, cart, checkout, thank-you page. Same design. Same domain. Same CRM.

It took less time than this post.

But here's the part most agencies will miss: that's not a feature. That's a product.

"I'll turn your funnel into a store this week" is something a local business will pay for. Setup fee, monthly care plan, done.

You don't need to sell all of HighLevel.

You need to sell one feature.

This is one.

— Andrew George · The One Feature guy · Founder, SaaSSuite

items.title: LinkedIn: Most agency owners pitch features.
items.body:
_Angle: the buyer. Image: story frame 4 or a product-list page screenshot._

Most agency owners pitch features.

But clients don't buy features. They buy "I can finally sell my thing online."

HighLevel just made that pitch easy: you can now put a full store inside an existing funnel. One click builds the product list, product details, cart, checkout and thank-you pages, using the design that's already there.

Therefore the question isn't "how do I set it up." It's "who do I sell it to?"

Here's my short list:

→ Gyms and studios: day passes, class packs, merch.
→ Coaches: workbooks, templates, a paid mini-course.
→ Local shops: gift cards and best-sellers, without a separate Shopify.
→ Restaurants and cafés: merch, sauces, catering deposits.
→ Churches and nonprofits: donations and event tickets on one page.

Every one of these already has a funnel or a website. But most of them don't have a way to take money on it.

That gap is your offer.

Pick one niche from that list. Build one demo store. Show it on the sales call.

One feature. One niche. One demo.

That's how you start a SaaS on HighLevel.

items.title: LinkedIn: I've watched hundreds of people try to sell HighLevel.
items.body:
_Angle: what this says about how to grow. Image: Andrew on stage (photo library stage-1)._

I've watched hundreds of people try to sell HighLevel.

The ones who stall all do the same thing: they sell the whole platform. CRM, calendars, automations, AI, reputation, funnels, all at once.

But the buyer hears "complicated," therefore they say "let me think about it."

The ones who grow do the opposite. They pick one feature and make it the whole offer.

Today's example: HighLevel stores can now live inside any funnel. Click an element, choose the sections, import — and a one-page funnel turns into a five-page store.

That single change is a complete offer:
• Who it's for: any local business with a funnel and something to sell.
• What it fixes: "I want to sell online but I don't want another platform."
• What you deliver: the store, live, in their branding, this week.

But one feature only works if you can explain it in one sentence.

Here's mine: "I'll turn your funnel into a store this week."

If you can't say your offer in one sentence, you're selling too much.

What's your one feature?

Therefore the pitch that closes is the boring one: one feature, one problem, one price.

Once it works, they ask what else you can do. That's when you show them the rest.

Start simple. Earn the upsell.

"If closing feels high pressure, you haven't sold them enough yet."

When someone's already in — they understand the problem, they trust you, they're happy — asking for payment isn't pressure. It's the next step.

So I do it live. "Here's the link. Let's get it taken care of." Then I stay on the call while they pay.

Positive → payment → reinforcement. Skip the last step and you'll feel it in refunds.

items.body:
Every salesperson has a graveyard of great calls.

The prospect laughed at your jokes. They agreed with everything. They said "we're ready." But then they needed time to think, and time turned into silence.

I spent my first years of sales in that graveyard, so I wrote myself a rule book. I called it Positive to Payment, and I recently walked through it on my podcast.

Every relationship has a give-to-ask ratio. Most people ask too soon, therefore the ask feels like a withdrawal from an account that was never funded. I call the balance perceived relationship equity. Your job on a first call isn't to pitch. It's to make deposits: be useful, listen, make them feel understood.

People pay when they (1) understand they have a problem, (2) trust you to fix it, and (3) have a way to pay you. The second one is where transparency wins. "We can fix your website" means nothing. "Here's how we'll fix it, and who does what" means everything. The third one sounds obvious, but it's where most "yes" calls die: the payment link isn't ready.

The more someone invests in the relationship — signing up for your lead magnet, watching your video, replying to your emails — the more likely they are to pay. That's why I like engagement scores: they turn "they seemed interested" into a number.

If they're in, send the link and stay with them while they pay. If that feels high pressure, you skipped a step. And after they pay, reinforce the decision. What you do in the hour after the sale protects the sale.

items.title: LinkedIn: "HighLevel is too complicated" is the most common objection I hear.
items.body:
_Image: Andrew on stage (photo library stage-2)._

"HighLevel is too complicated" is the most common objection I hear.

For years the honest answer was "yes, it is." You could train clients, record Looms, build help docs. But they still logged into a screen with every feature on it.

The new HighLevel UI changes the answer.

You can now decide what each client sees. Hide the sections they'll never use, pin the ones they need, and save that as a layout you apply across sub-accounts.

Therefore "too complicated" becomes a design choice you control.

But here's the lesson I'd take from it, beyond the feature: simplicity is the product.

Clients don't pay for more features. They pay for fewer decisions.

That's the whole idea behind SaaSSuite — one place for your clients to onboard, learn and get support. The new layouts are the same idea inside HighLevel itself.

What would you hide first?

items.title: Newsletter: There's a moment every HighLevel agency knows. The client logs in for …
items.body:
There's a moment every HighLevel agency knows. The client logs in for the first time, looks at the screen, and goes quiet.

They see twenty tabs. Pipelines, workflows, reputation, memberships, affiliate manager, AI studio. They came for a calendar and an inbox, but now they're looking at a cockpit. Therefore they close the tab and send you a text instead.

HighLevel's new UI is the first time the platform itself gives you a real fix.

Inside the new interface, the left-hand navigation has an Edit button. You can reorder tabs, hide whole sections, add quick links to the screens a client actually uses, rename categories and change icons. Then you save that layout and apply it to other sub-accounts.

You decide what your client sees.

"Too complicated" has always been HighLevel's biggest objection. You couldn't change the software, so you added training: Looms, help docs, onboarding calls. All useful. But the screen stayed the same.

Now the screen can change. A med spa gets Conversations, Calendar, Contacts and Reviews. A roofer gets Opportunities and the inbox. Nobody gets Affiliate Manager unless they asked for it.

- **The feature:** custom navigation layouts.
- **Who pays:** agencies with many clients in one niche, white-label SaaS builders, consultants with client portals.
- **What it sells:** "HighLevel, built for your industry." Fewer support tickets. Clients who log in.
- **How to deliver:** design one layout per niche, save it, apply it everywhere.

But a clean menu is only the first step. Clients still need to be onboarded, taught and supported. That's what I built

It's your automation raising its hand and saying: this one needs a person.

Add at least one manual action checkpoint to every pipeline stage.
